youtube_title: Cashing a 'Payment in Full' Check Can Settle a Disputed Bill 🦝⚖️
caption: Under UCC 3-311 (Nebraska's version shown), a good-faith check clearly offered as full payment of a genuinely disputed claim can settle it once cashed — with exceptions for designated addresses and repayment within 90 days.
script: Write payment in full on a check, and you might wipe out the rest of a bill you're fighting. [disclaimer] It's a real rule in American business law, and Nebraska's version is a good example. It's called accord and satisfaction. Fancy name, simple idea! Here's how it works. There has to be a real fight about how much is owed. Then the person paying sends a check in good faith as full payment. The check, or a note with it, has to clearly say it's payment in full. And then the person who's owed money cashes it. Boom. The rest of the bill can be wiped out! Picture this. A contractor bills you two thousand dollars. You honestly think the work was bad, so you send a check for fifteen hundred, clearly marked payment in full. If the contractor cashes it, the fight may be over! But writing payment in full isn't magic. If there's no real fight, and you just owe the bill, it doesn't work. Companies can set up a special address for these checks, and if yours doesn't go there, it may not count. And a company that cashes it can often undo it by paying the money back within ninety days. [loop] So before you cash that check marked payment in full, remember
